h1: What whisky colour does not tell you
title: What Whisky Colour Does Not Tell You | Craft Beer School
desc: Why a darker whisky is not always older or better: cask type, refill casks, climate and added caramel colouring all change colour without changing age.
teaser: Dark whisky looks old and rich. Sometimes it is. Sometimes a spoonful of caramel did the work.
standfirst: We drink with our eyes first. A deep amber whisky feels like a promise of age and richness. Colour is a weak clue, though. Cask type, climate and added colouring can all move it without telling you anything about age or quality.
sections:
Spirit comes off the still as clear as water. Every bit of colour in a mature whisky comes from the cask or from colouring added before bottling. The oak gives up compounds over time that tint the spirit from pale straw to deep mahogany. Our guide to tannin and colour from the cask explains the chemistry.

So colour does tell you something real: how much the cask has given to the spirit. What it does not tell you is how long that took or how good the result is.
The cask matters more than the years

A cask's history changes colour far more than its age. Some examples:

  • New charred oak, used for bourbon, gives deep colour fast. A four year old bourbon can be darker than a 15 year old Scotch.
  • First fill ex-sherry casks often give a rich red brown tone.
  • First fill ex-bourbon casks give gold to amber.
  • Refill casks, used two or three times, have given up much of their colour. A 20 year old whisky from a tired refill cask can be pale straw.

Pale and old or dark and young are both common. Neither tells you which you are holding.
Heat speeds colour as well as flavour

Climate changes the pace too. In a hot warehouse, spirit expands into the oak and draws back out as temperatures swing, pulling colour and flavour from the wood faster. Indian single malts can reach a deep amber in a few years that a cool Scottish warehouse might take a decade or more to match. Our guide to temperature swings in Indian warehouses covers why.

That is one more reason to compare colour only within a single climate and cask type, if at all.
Caramel colouring is allowed in many whiskies

Scotch whisky may contain plain caramel colouring, known as E150a, to adjust colour. It is permitted in many other whisky categories too. It is widely used in blends and some single malts. Its job is consistency: casks vary in colour while a brand wants every bottle on the shelf to look the same.

The amount used is small. Whether it changes flavour is argued about; at typical doses most tasters struggle to tell. What it certainly changes is what colour can tell you. Once caramel is involved, colour says nothing about the cask.

Bourbon is an exception. Rules for bourbon do not allow added colouring, so its colour comes from the new charred oak alone. Some Scotch and Indian labels state natural colour or no added colouring. That is the only way to know.
Why brands care so much about colour

A blend sold in millions of bottles is made from hundreds of casks. Each cask is a slightly different shade. Without adjustment, one batch might look noticeably paler than the last. Drinkers notice. Many assume a paler batch is weaker or has been changed, even when it tastes the same.

Colouring solves a marketing problem, not a flavour problem. That is worth keeping in mind on an Indian shop shelf, where a deep amber hue is often used to signal richness and age on the label and in the advertising. The honest question to ask of any bottle is simple: what would this look like without help? Only the label, or the producer, can answer it.
What colour can still tell you

Colour is not useless. Within one distillery's range, with natural colour stated, a darker whisky has probably spent more time in more active casks. A red tinge often points to sherry or red wine casks. A very pale whisky with a big age statement suggests refill casks and a spirit led style.

Treat colour as a question, not an answer. Look at it, guess, then nose and taste to find out. Your nose is a far better witness than your eyes.
Try a blind tasting in dark glasses

Professional panels sometimes taste from dark or blue glasses so colour cannot bias them. Without seeing the whisky, people often rate a pale one higher or guess ages very differently. It is a humbling exercise and worth doing once.

At home, ask a friend to pour three whiskies into identical opaque cups or simply blindfold you. Guess the age and cask type of each. The gap between what you expect from colour and what you actually find is the gap a structured sensory course closes.

Check the labels of the whiskies you own for the words natural colour or no added colouring. Line up the ones that say so. Order them by colour, then taste them and order them by how much oak you find. Compare the two lines. The mismatches are where colour was misleading you.
faqs: Does darker whisky mean older whisky?
No. Cask type, how many times the cask was used and climate all change colour. Many whiskies also contain caramel colouring.
Is caramel colouring allowed in whisky?
Plain caramel colouring is permitted in Scotch and many other whiskies to keep colour consistent. Bourbon does not allow added colouring.
How can I tell if a whisky has added colour?
Look for natural colour or no added colouring on the label. If it does not say, assume it may contain caramel.
